summary.text: Gene regulation is the range of mechanisms cells use to increase or decrease the production of specific gene products, which are proteins or RNA.
It lets cells make a protein only when it is needed, for example to respond to the environment or adapt to a new food source, in viruses, prokaryotes and eukaryotes alike.
In multicellular organisms it drives the creation of different cell types, each with its own pattern of gene activity, from the same genome sequence.

facts.label: What it controls
facts.value: How much protein or RNA a gene produces

facts.label: Gene silencing
facts.value: DNA methylation is a common method of silencing

facts.label: Enhancers
facts.value: Much more common in eukaryotes than in prokaryotes

items.prompt: A heart cell and a skin cell from the same person hold the same DNA sequence, yet they look and work very differently. What explains this?

options.label: Each cell type keeps a different set of chromosomes
The heart cell deletes the genes it doesn't need
Each cell type uses its genes in its own pattern
Cell types differ only because of their surroundings

items.explain: Gene regulation drives differentiation, creating cell types with different gene expression profiles from the same genome sequence.

items.prompt: A protein attaches to DNA near a gene's start site and blocks RNA polymerase from moving along the strand. What happens to that gene?

options.label: Less of its product is made
More of its product is made
Its DNA sequence is rewritten
Nothing changes in the gene's output

items.explain: A repressor binds near the promoter and impedes RNA polymerase's progress, which impedes expression of the gene.

items.prompt: In a stretch of DNA, methylation and histone deacetylation work together and the DNA gets packed more densely than before. What do you expect for the genes there?

options.label: They get transcribed more often
They get copied twice as fast
Their sequences get shorter
They get transcribed less often

items.explain: The combination of the two seems to signal denser packing, and denser packing generally goes with less frequent transcription and lower expression.

items.prompt: Chemical changes to genomic DNA and histones can alter how active a gene is without altering the DNA or RNA sequence. What are these changes called?

options.label: Point mutations
Epigenetic modifications
Frame shifts
Gene duplications

items.explain: Epigenetics refers to modification of genes that does not change the DNA or RNA sequence, and these modifications are a key factor in influencing gene expression.

items.prompt: A bacterium lands in a place where a new kind of food is available. How does gene regulation help it?

options.label: It rewrites the cell's DNA to fit the food
It keeps every protein at its top level all the time
It stops the cell from changing its protein output
It lets the cell make the needed proteins when required

items.explain: Gene regulation lets cells adapt to new food sources by expressing protein when needed, which adds to an organism's versatility and adaptability.

items.prompt: A student claims a cell can only control a gene at the moment transcription begins. How should you respond?

options.label: Right, since later steps can't be adjusted
Right, since RNA is never changed once made
Wrong, because almost any step can be adjusted, even after the protein is made
Wrong, because control happens only after the protein is finished

items.explain: Virtually any step of gene expression can be modulated, from transcriptional initiation to RNA processing to post-translational modification of a protein.

paragraphs.heading: Turning genes up and down
paragraphs.text: A gene's product is the protein or RNA it is used to make. Gene regulation is the whole set of ways a cell raises or lowers how much of a particular product it makes. Almost every step on the way from gene to finished product can be adjusted, from the start of transcription, through processing of the RNA, to later modification of the protein. Often one regulator controls another, which controls another, forming a gene regulatory network.

paragraphs.heading: Why cells need it
paragraphs.text: Viruses, prokaryotes and eukaryotes all depend on gene regulation. It makes an organism more flexible, because the cell can make a protein when it is needed. Cells use it to set off developmental programs, react to their surroundings, or adjust to a new food source. In an embryo of a many-celled organism, it drives the formation of different cell types, each switching on its own mix of genes, even though all of them share the same genome.

paragraphs.heading: Packing DNA tightly or loosely
paragraphs.text: DNA is wound around groups of eight proteins called histones, and each such bundle is called a nucleosome. How densely the DNA is packed generally signals how often it is transcribed, that is, copied by RNA polymerase. In eukaryotes, chemical changes to histones can alter this structure and how reachable large stretches of DNA are, raising or lowering a gene's activity. Histone acetylation is one such change: enzymes called histone acetyltransferases free DNA from the histones so transcription can go ahead.

paragraphs.heading: Silencing with methyl tags
paragraphs.text: Adding methyl groups to DNA is a common way to silence a gene. Enzymes usually place these tags on cytosine bases within short CpG sequences. Methylation often works together with histone deacetylation, and the pair seems to signal the DNA to pack more densely, lowering gene activity. Abnormal methylation patterns are thought to play a part in the development of cancer.

paragraphs.heading: Switches near the gene
paragraphs.text: Several kinds of regulator change how readily RNA polymerase binds to a gene's promoter, a DNA region it can attach to. Repressors bind to a nearby site called the operator and get in the polymerase's way, so the gene stays quiet. Activators do the reverse, making the polymerase more strongly drawn to the promoter. Activators can bind to enhancers, DNA sites that loop round to bring a promoter to the starting machinery, while silencers are DNA regions that, once certain transcription factors bind them, can shut a gene off.

paragraphs.heading: Changes that can be passed on
paragraphs.text: Some of the tags that control gene activity can be inherited, and this is called epigenetic regulation. Epigenetics means changing how genes behave without changing the DNA or RNA sequence itself. Such changes sit on the DNA and on histones. RNA molecules can also act as regulators, including microRNA and long non-coding RNA, and some long non-coding RNAs are linked to Parkinson, Huntington and Alzheimer disease.
